projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Carl Evans was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Kerri Arsenault
sp.p: This is March 25th, 2004. My name is Kerri Arsenault, and I am interviewing Carl Evans at his home at 147 Lenfield Avenue in Middletown, Rhode Island, zip code 02842. Also attending this interview is Carl's grand daughter, Casey Smith. Carl served in the Navy as Chief Boat Trainee and served in San Diego and Long Beach, California; Norfolk, Virginia; New London, Connecticut, and Newport, Rhode Island. When were you drafted or where did you enlist?

sp.speaker: Kerri Arsenault
sp.p: When were you drafted or where did you enlist?

sp.speaker: Kerri Arsenault
sp.p: Portland, Oregon. And where were you living at the time?

sp.speaker: Carl Evans
sp.p: It was just what I wanted to do.

sp.speaker: Kerri Arsenault
sp.p: Okay. And why did you pick the service or branch that you joined, why the Navy?

sp.speaker: Carl Evans
sp.p: Why did I choose the Navy?

sp.speaker: Carl Evans
sp.p: I was always interested in the Navy from the time I was a kid.

sp.speaker: Kerri Arsenault
sp.p: And what did it feel like to enlist?

sp.speaker: Kerri Arsenault
sp.p: What did it feel like to enlist?

sp.speaker: Carl Evans
sp.p: What, when I joined the Navy?

sp.speaker: Kerri Arsenault
sp.p: Did you go through boot camp or training?

sp.speaker: Kerri Arsenault
sp.p: Boot camp. What was like that like?

sp.speaker: Carl Evans
sp.p: San Diego, California, and it was great.

sp.speaker: Kerri Arsenault
sp.p: Do you remember what your instructors were like?

sp.speaker: Kerri Arsenault
sp.p: Do you remember what your instructors were like?

sp.speaker: Carl Evans
sp.p: Well, I had a couple old chiefs, and I don't know what their names were now.

sp.speaker: Carl Evans
sp.p: And then when I was a third-class recruit petty officer before I got out of there while I was in the Navy --

sp.speaker: Carl Evans
sp.p: -- I did all right in boot camp.

sp.speaker: Kerri Arsenault
sp.p: And was it tough to get through?

sp.speaker: Kerri Arsenault
sp.p: Was it tough to get through it?

sp.speaker: Kerri Arsenault
sp.p: Okay. And you said -- where did you serve in or you enlisted?

sp.speaker: Carl Evans
sp.p: Went to San Diego, California for recruit training. It took three months. I graduated from there an apprentice seaman, then a private -- (Music playing) -- went aboard the USS Bravos --

sp.speaker: Carl Evans
sp.p: -- and then transferred to the USS Colorado, a battleship.

sp.speaker: Carl Evans
sp.p: And the next ship was the USS Idaho, and I stayed on that one for three years.

sp.speaker: Carl Evans
sp.p: And then I got a transport -- where were we at -- we were at Guantanamo Bay. I got on the USS Shalimar, rode that to Norfolk, Virginia. Then I spent some time in the receiving station, and then got transferred to Brooklyn, New York. And in Brooklyn, New York, I caught new construction --

sp.speaker: Carl Evans
sp.p: -- USS Vixin. I rode that for a couple of years or so. My next ship was the USS Wichita, which was a brand new ship. The next ship after that was the USS Deegan. (Laughter.) (Birds chirping) That was for the birds. (Laughter.) That was a cargo ship.

sp.speaker: Carl Evans
sp.p: That was the best ship I was ever on.

sp.speaker: Kerri Arsenault
sp.p: What was your job or assignment when you were on the ship?

sp.speaker: Kerri Arsenault
sp.p: Okay. And was it tough to keep in touch with your family all of that time when you were away from home?

sp.speaker: Carl Evans
sp.p: That's when I wasn't married then.

sp.speaker: Kerri Arsenault
sp.p: Uh-huh. What was the food like on that ship?

sp.speaker: Kerri Arsenault
sp.p: And were there plenty of supplies?

sp.speaker: Kerri Arsenault
sp.p: Were there plenty of supplies on the ship?

sp.speaker: Kerri Arsenault
sp.p: At any point did you feel pressure to --

sp.speaker: Carl Evans
sp.p: Well, before that we didn't have good food, but we had good food on those battleships. (Laughter) --

sp.speaker: Carl Evans
sp.p: -- and we had one commissary store on that cargo ship. (Unidentified voices in background) (Laughter.)

sp.speaker: Carl Evans
sp.p: -- we had swordfish steaks every Friday for a long time.

sp.speaker: Kerri Arsenault
sp.p: Wow, that's awesome. Was there something special that you did for good luck?

sp.speaker: Carl Evans
sp.p: Yes, I used to pray a lot.

sp.speaker: Kerri Arsenault
sp.p: And how did the people on that ship entertain themselves at that time?

sp.speaker: Carl Evans
sp.p: How did you entertain yourself aboard ship?

sp.speaker: Carl Evans
sp.p: We played cards. We listened to the radio.

sp.speaker: Kerri Arsenault
sp.p: Was there entertainers there, did people come on the ship?

sp.speaker: Kerri Arsenault
sp.p: Okay. What did you do when you were on leave? (Laughter)

sp.speaker: Kerri Arsenault
sp.p: Uh-huh. Anything in particular, or anything in particular?

sp.speaker: Kerri Arsenault
sp.p: I understand that. Where was your favorite place that you traveled in the service?

sp.speaker: Carl Evans
sp.p: Oh, I guess Honolulu, I guess.

sp.speaker: Kerri Arsenault
sp.p: Wow, that's awesome. And do you recall any particularly humorous or unusual events, anything that stands out in your mind?

sp.speaker: Carl Evans
sp.p: Well -- (laughter) I guess the weirdest thing that happened, we'd lost three sea planes in one day --

sp.speaker: Carl Evans
sp.p: -- off a battleship. We lot another one in the San Francisco Bay.

sp.speaker: Kerri Arsenault
sp.p: Any pranks, any practical jokes that you remember?

sp.speaker: Carl Evans
sp.p: Well, there weren't too many jokers aboard ship.

sp.speaker: Kerri Arsenault
sp.p: Uh-huh. Everyone was pretty serious. Do you have any photographs?

sp.speaker: Kerri Arsenault
sp.p: And who were in the photographs, just friends or --

sp.speaker: Carl Evans
sp.p: Oh, I got like a scrapbook with a lot of pictures in it --

sp.speaker: Carl Evans
sp.p: -- just different -- just a lot of different places.

sp.speaker: Kerri Arsenault
sp.p: Uh-huh. What did you think of the officers and the fellow people that you worked under?

sp.speaker: Carl Evans
sp.p: The officers that I worked under?

sp.speaker: Kerri Arsenault
sp.p: They were all right, no one gave you a really hard time or anything?

sp.speaker: Kerri Arsenault
sp.p: Did you keep a personal diary?

sp.speaker: Carl Evans
sp.p: Uh-huh. I got a scrapbook, yeah.

sp.speaker: Kerri Arsenault
sp.p: Uh-huh. Do you recall the day that your service ended?

sp.speaker: Kerri Arsenault
sp.p: The day your service ended, do you remember what the day was like when you were all finished?

sp.speaker: Carl Evans
sp.p: Yes. When I went into retirement?

sp.speaker: Carl Evans
sp.p: Yeah. December -- I think it was December the 5th, 1955.

sp.speaker: Kerri Arsenault
sp.p: Uh-huh. Where were you when you finished your service?

sp.speaker: Kerri Arsenault
sp.p: Is that why you moved here?

sp.speaker: Carl Evans
sp.p: Well, the navy brought me here.

sp.speaker: Kerri Arsenault
sp.p: Uh-huh. What did you do in the days and weeks afterwards? When you finally finished, what did you do?

sp.speaker: Kerri Arsenault
sp.p: And so did you have any education or anything supported by the GI Bill?

sp.speaker: Kerri Arsenault
sp.p: Did you make any close friendships while you were in the service that you kept?

sp.speaker: Kerri Arsenault
sp.p: Did you continue any of those friendships or relationships?

sp.speaker: Kerri Arsenault
sp.p: Did you continue any of those relationships? Do you still keep in touch with anybody?

sp.speaker: Carl Evans
sp.p: No, no. I have not kept up with any of my old shipmates.

sp.speaker: Kerri Arsenault
sp.p: Did you join any veteran organizations?

sp.speaker: Kerri Arsenault
sp.p: What did you go on to do?

sp.speaker: Carl Evans
sp.p: What did I go on to do? Well, we didn't have Fleet Reserve then. Years since then, I'm in the Fleet Reserve Association. I'm not in it right now.

sp.speaker: Kerri Arsenault
sp.p: Uh-huh. And what did you go on to do in your career after the war, after you finished?

sp.speaker: Carl Evans
sp.p: I went into the taxi business.

sp.speaker: Kerri Arsenault
sp.p: Did your military experience influence your thinking about war and the military in general?

sp.speaker: Kerri Arsenault
sp.p: Like did it influence your thinking about anything or change the way you think about the war now?

sp.speaker: Kerri Arsenault
sp.p: And if you were in a veterans' organization, do you have reunions or --

sp.speaker: Carl Evans
sp.p: I'm not in any veterans' association. I got a thing called the Fleet Reserve Association. That's for active and retired, so it's not really a veterans' association. It's members and retired members of the service, not really that is for retired veterans' organization.

sp.speaker: Kerri Arsenault
sp.p: Okay. How did your service and experience affect your life?

sp.speaker: Carl Evans
sp.p: How did it affect my life?

sp.speaker: Carl Evans
sp.p: Well, I guess I would say it made me a military man with a military mind and military thoughts and military actions and a military way of life.

sp.speaker: Kerri Arsenault
sp.p: So now do you still think that way?

sp.speaker: Kerri Arsenault
sp.p: Do you still think that way now?

sp.speaker: Kerri Arsenault
sp.p: Is there anything that you would like to add that we have not covered in the interview?

sp.speaker: Carl Evans
sp.p: Not a whole lot, maybe a little detail here and there, but nothing important.

sp.speaker: Kerri Arsenault
sp.p: Okay. Is that all you want to share?

sp.speaker: Kerri Arsenault
sp.p: Well, thank you so much for sharing your recollections with me.
